headline: The owner is right about roughly half of it, and the half he's right about is the more important half. On raw decision *power* we beat the proposal comprehensively — `eqmValidity` (app.js:1859) returns a three-level verdict with `okPaths`, `eqmDeviceMeetsRow`+`eqmFitVerdict` (equipment.js:145/256) check capability × capacity × ledger window, and `schedulePlacements` (app.js:3970) emits seven typed conflict reasons with a bounded pull — while their `Validate_Equipment_For_Cut` is a set-intersection on device-type strings and their `optimizeEvent` never reads equipment in its time loop. But on decision *architecture* they are genuinely ahead: they have ONE registry where a rule carries its own trigger, action class and explanation, and we have roughly thirteen separate decision sites each with a private verdict vocabulary and its own message rendering. The single sharpest proof is ours, not theirs: `validCombo` (app.js:1042) returns a bare boolean and the click handler at app.js:2986-2992 re-derives *why* it failed by re-inspecting `methodRules` — four hand-written messages, with the produce text as the fall-through, so adding one `invalid` entry to a non-produce class silently tells the user "For produce: up to 2 methods". And one correction the previous panel got factually wrong: we are not without telemetry — `copilotLogProbe`/`copilotPace`/`copilotStallInfo`/`copilotAdjustServe` (app.js:6765-6800) already do manual probe capture, stall detection, rate-based ETA and an ahead/behind verdict. What we lack is not sensing but *closure*: nothing re-runs the solver, and the session carries one `probes[]` for the whole cookout.

conceptsFound.concept: Rule registry — a rule set as an enumerable declarative table, each entry carrying trigger, action class, and its own user-facing explanation
conceptsFound.steelman: Every culinary/equipment/logistics decision the app makes is one row in a table with a stable id: {id, scope, when(ctx), act:{class, code, params}, cite}. The evaluator is ~10 lines. Consequences: you can list every rule the app knows; you can prove per-rule test coverage (fired + not-fired); adding a rule is adding a row, not editing an if-chain buried in a render path; the rule and its explanation cannot drift apart because they are the same object; and an AI can be handed the rule set as data without being trusted to produce it.
conceptsFound.value: We have ~13 decision sites — methodRules, validCombo, gearAwareDefault, eqmValidity, eqmDeviceMeetsRow, eqmFitVerdict, cookerContention, schedulePlacements(+_schedAdviceHtml), eqmAddGate/eqmAddGateKeys/eqmEventWindowCheck, gearMissingHelp, copilotAdviceLocal, safetyDiff, aiSafetyNote — each with its own verdict vocabulary ('ok/partial/missing', 'ok/blocked-default/uncookable', 'free/partial/busy', 7 conflict 'reason' strings, 4 toast strings, 'ahead/behind/on-pace'). One registry gives us a rules index, a coverage report, one place to add a rule, and one renderer — which is also the only way Guard A/B can ever see every decision string statically.

conceptsFound.concept: Action-class taxonomy: block / adjust / append-stage / warn
conceptsFound.steelman: A rule declares WHAT KIND of intervention it is, and the engine — not the rule author — decides what each class is allowed to touch. 'block' halts; 'warn' annotates; 'append-stage' adds a step; 'adjust' rewrites a parameter. The taxonomy is the safety boundary: you can ban an entire class of intervention structurally rather than per-rule.
conceptsFound.value: We have block and warn, we have enrich-without-change (equipPlan, app.js:1147, explicitly 'may ENRICH a stage, may never change one'), and we structurally FORBID adjust via safetyDiff (app.js:3920). But we have no append-stage class at all — itemStages (app.js:4093) is a monolithic combo if-chain, so no rule can add a stage to a plan. Their rule 6 (skin-on waterfowl → force skin-scoring + append a sear stage) is literally unrepresentable in our architecture without editing itemStages. Adopt the taxonomy, keep 'adjust' banned, add 'append-stage' constrained to CITED stage templates.

conceptsFound.concept: The rule owns its explanation — one object carries the trigger and the sentence
conceptsFound.steelman: 'Meat will be too tough. Requires long braising or smoking' lives on the same row as the condition that produced it. A new rule cannot ship without a message, and a message cannot be attached to the wrong rule.
conceptsFound.value: Fixes a real fragility: app.js:2986-2992 re-derives the failure reason from methodRules AFTER validCombo already computed it, with four messages and a produce-text fall-through. Non-produce `invalid` entries would get the wrong sentence. Also fixes the disabled-toggle case (app.js:1193) where four distinct culinary reasons — produce over-cook, gizzard pre-tenderize, collagen-needs-cook, steak-any-combo — all render as the same five-word tooltip 'Not available for this item'.

conceptsFound.concept: Acquisition remedy — the engine names WHAT TO BUY to unblock, not just what is missing (§11 scenario ב')
conceptsFound.steelman: A blocked verdict returns {reason, suggested_remedy, acquisition} — 'cheddar needs cold smoke <30°C; your oven and grill run too hot; get a cold-smoke spiral for an unlit grill'. The blocker is stated as a physical constraint, the remedy as a specific purchasable capability.
conceptsFound.value: We already have the CONTENT — gearMissingHelp (app.js:1161-1183) gives alternative technique + texture trade-off + a `buy:` line per missing method. What we lack is the ARCHITECTURE: it is hardcoded to three methods, reachable only from the method-toggle strip, and completely unknown to eqInvPanelHtml (app.js:1971), whose fixes are configure / switch-path / a disabled E5 placeholder. So a user blocked by eqmValidity never sees the buy advice that already exists twenty lines away. Unify both into one 'offer' finding class.

conceptsFound.concept: Validate_Equipment_For_Cut — INTERSECT required-alternatives × owned kit → return the ACHIEVABLE methods (data-driven substitution)
conceptsFound.steelman: Each cut declares REQUIRED_ALTERNATIVES as data; the engine intersects with owned equipment and returns the set of methods that actually work, so 'what can I cook and how' is one function over data rather than logic spread across the app.
conceptsFound.value: gearAwareDefault (app.js:1028) enumerates all seven method subsets, filters by per-cut culinary rules (validCombo), then by gearCan; eqmValidity.okPaths does the same per cited path with capability and capacity checks their version has none of. Ours is strictly stronger. BUT their substitution policy is DATA and ours is CODE — cookerCandidates (app.js:281) hardcodes smoke→smoker|charcoal/kettle/gas-grill, cook→grill|oven. And we already authored the data version: equipment_map.py emits equip.alt = {"smoker":["grill"]} / {"grill":["smoker"]} per recipe and NOTHING in app.js reads it. That is live dead data — the ladder exists and is unwired.

conceptsFound.concept: Preference → path routing (PREFERENCE_TEXTURE/PREFERENCE_FLAVOR → PROCESS_FLOW; §8's three outcome buttons)
conceptsFound.steelman: The user states the OUTCOME they want — fall-apart / crisp-and-traditional / fast — and the engine selects among the available process routes. Method choice becomes a consequence of a stated goal instead of a technique the user must already know.
conceptsFound.value: Our path selection has exactly two inputs today: gear (gearAwareDefault) and a manual method toggle (activeMethods/cardMethods). There is no function anywhere that maps a desired outcome onto a path. This is a decision-engine gap, and it can be built with ZERO invented numbers — score the already-cited itemPaths by an outcome vector derived from fields we already hold (svt/svh vs smt/soh for tenderness and time, wrap for bark, sear for crust, tgt for chew). It is the natural router form of CP2's path panel.

conceptsFound.concept: Device failure as a first-class event that triggers re-planning, with a backup ladder (handleDeviceFailure)
conceptsFound.steelman: A device flips to FAULT; every item assigned to it is re-allocated down an ordered ladder (free oven → covered grill → fail), each rung carrying a culinary justification ('the meat already absorbed its smoke, so an oven finish costs nothing'). The plan repairs itself instead of merely reporting a broken state.
conceptsFound.value: We have no device availability state at all. EQUIP_CATS carries 19 properties and none of them is 'is this device working'. EQM.availability reasons only about ledger occupancy; eqmReleaseByDevice exists solely for deletion. Mid-cook hardware failure is the single most common real BBQ crisis and we cannot represent it. Our ladder would be strictly better than theirs because cookerCandidates + eqmDeviceMeetsRow already know which surviving device can actually reach the temp and hold the footprint — theirs picks any idle OVEN.

conceptsFound.concept: Closed telemetry loop: reading → prediction → decision → re-plan (stall→wrap, ready-early→cooler, predicted-late→speed-up)
conceptsFound.steelman: Sensor state is compared against the plan on every update; a divergence produces a typed action, and the action feeds back into the schedule so the whole timeline re-derives. The plan is a live object, not a printout.
conceptsFound.value: CORRECTION to the previous panel: we DO sense. copilotLogProbe/copilotPace/copilotStallInfo (app.js:6755-6800) give manual probe capture, stall detection grounded in vetted troubleshooting content, °C/h rate, ETA, and an ahead/behind/on-pace verdict against serve minus rest — and copilotPace deliberately refuses to extrapolate through the stall, which is more honest than their blind projection. What is missing is CLOSURE: copilotAdjustServe (app.js:6769) writes mk-tlserve but never re-runs planSchedule/schedulePlacements/cookerContention, and a 'behind' verdict produces prose (copilotAdviceLocal) instead of moves. The gap is one wire, not a subsystem.

conceptsFound.concept: Per-ITEM live status machine (PENDING / COOKING / RESTING_HOLDING / SERVED / FAILED) on every menu item
conceptsFound.steelman: Live state is keyed by item, so a multi-item cookout tracks each cut's own probe series, target, device assignment and status independently — which is the precondition for per-item crisis handling and for the cooler-buffer move.
conceptsFound.value: Our live session (startLiveCook, app.js:6738) stores ONE probes[] and ONE targetC for the entire scope. A two-brisket cookout — the exact scenario the whole equipment/occupancy stack exists to serve — cannot be tracked. This is the cheapest structural fix on this list and it unblocks everything else in the live loop.

conceptsFound.concept: Insulated cooler (faux cambro) as a schedulable BUFFER resource, not just advice
conceptsFound.steelman: The cooler is a device with a holding profile: an item that hits target early transfers into it, which simultaneously frees a rack in the smoker and removes schedule pressure. Holding becomes a placement move the optimizer can choose.
conceptsFound.value: We already give the advice in prose (_copilotPaceHtml's 'ahead' branch and copilotAdviceLocal both say 'hold it wrapped in a cooler'), and equipment_map.py already emits a 'cooler' token as `opt` for cooks ≥4h and rests ≥30min. But the cooler is not a device in EQUIP_CATS, so it can never free rack area in schedulePlacements or be chosen by the Phase-3a hold rung. Making it a real device with a hold profile turns existing prose into an optimizer move. Note: Phase-3a's safety spine (60°C floor, 240-min danger-zone budget, holdCapMin 360) already exists as approved design and is far more careful than their unbounded 4-8h claim.

conceptsFound.concept: Method conversion with an explicit gain/loss attribute vector (LOSS_OF_ATTR / GAIN_OF_ATTR + time factor)
conceptsFound.steelman: Switching route is presented as a trade: this route costs you bark and smoke aroma and buys you juiciness and 88% of the clock. The user chooses on consequences rather than on technique names.
conceptsFound.value: Already picked by the prior panel for CP2, but on this lens it is more than a display: the same vector is the SCORING INPUT for the preference router above. Build it once as pathOutcome(meta, pathId) and it serves both. Their time-conversion COEFFICIENTS must be rejected outright — sous-vide duration is a pasteurization value and may never be multiplied.

conceptsFound.concept: Cross-layer interaction rules (flavor × physics): sous-vide + liquid sauce → remove from bag and reduce separately; no oil in the bag; −30% spice in vacuum; no sugar above 120°C during smoke-ring formation
conceptsFound.steelman: The flavor layer is a plugin, but the plugin's APPLICATION is governed by the physical method. A small set of interaction rules is what makes the separation of variables actually work instead of producing nonsense combinations.
conceptsFound.value: Verified gap: injectSeasoningSteps(steps, key, tmpl) (app.js:1273) never receives the combo. Our glaze timing is a fixed 'last 10-15 minutes' regardless of method (app.js:1288, and the work-plan task at app.js:7273 pins it to lastCook.end−15min), and our sauce step is method-blind. seasoningsFor already does protein↔profile matching, so the compatibility half is ours; the method-interaction half is entirely absent. This is a small, safe, high-visibility set of rules and it is the first real customer for the registry.

conceptsFound.concept: Per-device smoke-intensity coefficient and fuel-type recommendation as decision inputs
conceptsFound.steelman: Device class is not just capacity — an offset burning splits and a pellet grill are different smoke instruments, and the engine adjusts wood quantity/duration guidance accordingly.
conceptsFound.value: We have DEVICE_FUEL and REFUEL_MIN (app.js:1127-1141) feeding equipPlan with fuel notes and refuel cadence, and per-type smokerTip strings — richer operationally than their single float. What we lack is any notion of smoke INTENSITY differing by device. Low priority on this lens; worth noting only because it is a decision input we could carry once the registry exists, and any coefficient must be cited.

conceptsFound.concept: Consumables calculator that emits a REASON per line item
conceptsFound.steelman: Not 'buy 9kg charcoal' but 'buy 9kg charcoal — 0.8 kg/h × 9 hours + 20% margin for wind and cold'. Every quantity is auditable by the user against their own conditions.
conceptsFound.value: Prior panel picked the calculator; the part worth stealing on THIS lens is the reason field. It is the same discipline as our gaps/fixes codes — an output that explains its own derivation. Their consumption rates are uncited and must be replaced.

conceptsFound.concept: Four-step decision funnel as the UI contract (raw material → compatible flavor profiles only → outcome route → operating dashboard)
conceptsFound.steelman: Each step narrows the feasible set using the previous answer, so the user is never offered an option the engine will later reject. The engine's feasible-set computation IS the navigation.
conceptsFound.value: We filter flavor by protein (seasoningsFor) and gate methods by gear (gearCan, the 🔒 tag) — so steps 1, 2 and 4 exist. Step 3 (outcome route) is the missing one, and it is the same gap as the preference router. Worth stating as an architectural principle: never render an option the engine will block; block-at-the-gate (eqmAddGate's toast) is our current fallback and it is the worse pattern.

conceptsFound.concept: Blocked verdict states the physical constraint that caused it, not just the missing device kind
conceptsFound.steelman: 'Cheddar requires cold smoke below 30°C; your oven and grill cannot go that low' — the reason is a temperature relationship between the food and the kit, so the user learns the physics and can reason about substitutes we did not enumerate.
conceptsFound.value: Our gaps are {kind, state} — 'Smoker: missing', 'Probe: missing'. Correct, translatable, and code-shaped (which is right), but the WHY stops at the device kind. eqmDeviceMeetsRow already knows the exact failing predicate (maxTempC floor, bathMinL, hang, probe) and throws that information away when it returns false. Returning the failed predicate as the gap's `cause` code is nearly free and makes our messages match theirs in explanatory depth while staying prose-free.

whereItBeatsUs:
Plainly: on decision *architecture*, in five specific places.

1. **One registry vs thirteen decision sites.** Their seven rules are one enumerable table. Ours are scattered across `methodRules`/`validCombo` (app.js:989/1042), `gearAwareDefault` (1028), `eqmValidity` (1859), `eqmDeviceMeetsRow`/`eqmFitVerdict` (equipment.js:145/256), `cookerContention` (306), `schedulePlacements`+`_schedAdviceHtml` (3970/4063), `eqmAddGate`/`eqmAddGateKeys`/`eqmEventWindowCheck` (2060/2084/2031), `gearMissingHelp` (1161), `copilotAdviceLocal` (6820). Each invented its own verdict vocabulary. There is no place to add a rule, no way to list the rules, and no rules-coverage report.

2. **Our rules do not carry their explanations, and it is already provably fragile.** `validCombo` returns a bare boolean; app.js:2986-2992 then re-derives the reason by re-inspecting `methodRules` with four hand-written messages whose fall-through is the produce text — so any `invalid` entry added to a non-produce class ships "For produce: up to 2 methods" to the user. Worse, `methodToggleHTML` (app.js:1193) collapses four distinct culinary reasons into one tooltip, "Not available for this item". Their rule 1 says *why*: "Meat will be too tough. Requires long braising or smoking." On this specific comparison they are simply better and it costs us nothing to match.

3. **No append-stage action class.** `itemStages` (app.js:4093) is a single monolithic combo if-chain. No rule anywhere can add a stage to a plan. Their rule 6 — skin-on waterfowl forces skin-scoring and appends a sear stage if no sear exists — is unrepresentable for us without editing itemStages by hand. This is the structural reason our "flavor layer" is method-blind too: `injectSeasoningSteps` (app.js:1273) never receives the combo, so we cannot express "sous-vide + liquid sauce → take it out of the bag and reduce it separately".

4. **Device failure does not exist in our model, so the plan cannot repair itself.** `EQUIP_CATS` carries 19 device properties and not one of them is availability. `EQM.availability` reasons only about the ledger; `eqmReleaseByDevice` exists solely for deletion. Their `handleDeviceFailure` re-allocates every affected item down an ordered backup ladder with a culinary justification per rung. We would emit nothing at all.

5. **Our telemetry loop does not close, and it is per-session rather than per-item.** `copilotAdjustServe` (app.js:6769) writes `mk-tlserve` and never re-runs `planSchedule`/`schedulePlacements`/`cookerContention`; `copilotPace`'s "behind" verdict renders prose from `copilotAdviceLocal`, not moves. And `startLiveCook` (app.js:6738) stores one `probes[]` and one `targetC` for the whole scope, so a two-item cookout — the exact case the entire equipment/occupancy stack was built for — cannot be tracked. Their `FleetMenu[]` with per-item `status`/`target_internal`/`est_time_remaining` is the better shape.

One more, smaller but real: **their substitution policy is data, ours is code — and we already wrote the data and never wired it.** `equipment_map.py` emits `equip.alt = {"smoker": ["grill"]}` and `{"grill": ["smoker"]}` per recipe; nothing in app.js reads `equip.alt`. The same policy is hardcoded in `cookerCandidates` (app.js:281). That is a live dead-data finding surfaced by this comparison.
whereWeAreBetter:
Concretely, and I can defend each one:

**Verdict richness.** `eqmValidity` (app.js:1859) distinguishes `blocked-default` from `uncookable` and returns `okPaths` — "your default route is blocked but this other cited route works". Their engine `throw`s a single Error. That distinction is the difference between crying wolf on 109 catalog items and not.

**Feasibility depth.** Their `INTERSECT(REQUIRED_ALTERNATIVES, USER_EQUIPMENT)` is set membership over device-type strings. `eqmDeviceMeetsRow` (equipment.js:145) additionally checks the device's `maxC` against the cited stage temperature, bath volume via `chooseBath`, hanging via `deviceCanHang`, and standalone probe satisfaction; `eqmFitVerdict` (equipment.js:256) then checks whole-device area sum, a per-slot floor that branches on measured-vs-estimated tolerance, bath-volume max-not-sum, and one-circulator-one-temperature exclusivity — over ledger holds in a half-open time window. Their engine cannot know a 135°C electric smoker fails a 160°C stage, nor that a 1320 cm² brisket fits no single shelf of a 5-shelf cabinet.

**Scheduling.** `schedulePlacements` (app.js:3970) does latest-first resource-constrained placement with slack, seven typed conflict codes (`temp-ceiling`, `no-single-slot`, `no-window`, `bath-temp`, `bath-too-small`, `hooks`, `pull-too-far`), and a bounded pull (`SCHED_PULL_MAX_MS`) that refuses to silently schedule food to finish 12 hours before dinner. Their `optimizeEvent` computes each item's start independently, never reads `equipment` inside that loop, and sorts by a formatted-time string.

**Codes, not prose.** Our verdicts are `{kind:'smoker', state:'missing'}` / `{reason:'no-single-slot', cm2, perSlotCm2}` and the sentence is built at the render layer with static `L()` literals, so Guards A/B/C see every string. Their engine interpolates Hebrew prose inside business logic and persists rendered prose into `live_timeline`.

**The "adjust" ban is architecture, not discipline.** `safetyDiff` (app.js:3920) compares a plan against its own pre-transform self on kind/hours/temp/safe and is a runtime invariant, and `equipPlan` (app.js:1147) is documented as enrich-only. Their rules 4 and 7 silently rewrite the user's target temperature. We should keep this ban permanently and write it into the registry as a forbidden action class.

**Honest live math.** `copilotPace` (app.js:6779) explicitly refuses to project an ETA through the stall (`rate<=1 && 65<=T<=77 → state:'stall'`) rather than emitting a wild number, and `copilotStallInfo` cites the app's own troubleshooting guide in the UI. Their `processTelemetry` projects blindly from `est_time_remaining_mins`.

**Chewiness modelling.** Their rule 1 has one flag, `collagen_level: HIGH|LOW`. `methodRules` (app.js:989) branches into four culinary classes — produce (all-three-together over-cooks), offal with a gizzard sub-case that *requires* sous-vide pre-tenderizing, doneness-bearing steak cuts (any combination legal), and collagen/long cuts (grill legal only as a finish) — with per-class `allowed`/`def`/`require`/`needsCookFor`/`invalid`. That is a strictly richer chewiness model. Its only failing is that it does not say so out loud.
proposedModel:
**A `RULES` registry + one `decide()` evaluator, in a new `rules.js` inlined before `app.js` exactly as `equipment.js` is (ruling F5/H2), wrapping existing functions rather than rewriting them.**

**Rule shape** — declarative, enumerable, and structurally incapable of emitting prose or a number:
```js
{ id:'collagen-needs-long-cook', scope:'path',
  when: ctx => ctx.cut.collagen==='high' && ctx.combo.length===1 && ctx.combo[0]==='grill',
  act:  { class:'block', code:'CHEWY_RISK' },
  params: ctx => ({ cut: ctx.cut.n }),
  cite: 'baldwin-collagen' }        // must resolve in sources.py or the BUILD fails
```
`scope ∈ {path, kit, plan, live}`. `when` is pure. `params` returns primitives only.

**Exactly four action classes; `adjust` is deliberately not one of them.**
- `block {code, params}` — halts.
- `warn {code, params, severity}` — annotates.
- `append-stage {templateId}` — may append only a stage template whose temp/hours come from a cited field; the build rejects a template with a literal number. Guarded at runtime by `safetyDiff` asserting append-only.
- `offer {code, options:[{type:'switch-path'|'reassign'|'configure'|'acquire', ...}]}` — the unified remedy class.

**Evaluator and renderer:**
```js
function decide(ctx){ return RULES.filter(r=>r.scope===ctx.scope)
  .map(r => r.when(ctx) ? {ruleId:r.id, ...r.act, params:r.params?r.params(ctx):{}} : null)
  .filter(Boolean); }
function renderFindings(findings)   // THE one code→L(he,en) table; nothing else renders a finding
```
Every user-facing decision string lives in that single table, so Guard A/B cover 100% of decision copy by construction.

**Migration — six waves, none touching a cited safety value:**

- **R0 (cheap, fixes a real bug).** `comboVerdict(c, combo) → {ok, findings}`; keep `validCombo(c,combo)` as `comboVerdict(c,combo).ok` so ~all call sites are untouched (the same delegation pattern Phase-3a's PREFS uses for `uiLevel`/`themeKey`). Move the four messages out of app.js:2986-2992 into codes. RED test: a non-produce class carrying an `invalid` entry must receive its OWN code, not `PRODUCE_OVERCOOK`. Also give `methodToggleHTML`'s disabled toggles their real reason code instead of "Not available for this item".
- **R1 (adoption, zero behaviour change).** Rename `schedulePlacements`' `conflicts[].reason` → `code` (they are already seven codes), express `eqmValidity.gaps` as findings (`EQ_MISSING`/`EQ_PARTIAL`/`EQ_PROBE`), and route `_schedAdviceHtml`, `eqInvPanelHtml`, and the `eqmAddGate` toasts through `renderFindings`. Four vocabularies collapse into one. Snapshot tests must show byte-identical output.
- **R2 (the `offer` class).** One `remediesFor(finding)` merging today's three disconnected remedy sources: `eqmValidity.fixes` (configure/switch-path), `gearMissingHelp`'s alternative + trade-off + `buy:`, and — finally reading it — `equip.alt` from `equipment_map.py`. Add `cause` to each gap by returning the failing predicate from `eqmDeviceMeetsRow` instead of a bare `false`, so a block can say "your smoker tops out at 135° and this stage cites 160°" rather than "Smoker: missing".
- **R3 (`append-stage`).** Refactor `itemStages`' combo branches into a table of cited stage templates, then allow rules to append: sous-vide-and-crust-wanted → cited finish; skin-on waterfowl → cited sear. Gate: `safetyDiff` must report additive-only, and any template whose temp/hours is not traceable to a cited field is rejected at build time.
- **R4 (the preference router — the owner's §8 step 3).** `pathOutcome(meta, pathId) → {tender, bark, smoke, chew, hours}`, every component derived from fields we already hold (`svt/svh` vs `smt/soh`, `wrap`, `sear`, `tgt`, `doneness`) — no new numbers. Then `routeForOutcome(meta, {texture:'fall-apart', crust:'crisp', speed:'fast'}) → ranked itemPaths`. This is simultaneously CP2's path panel, the proposal's four-step funnel, and the gain/loss vector the prior panel picked — one mechanism, three deliverables.
- **R5 (close the live loop).** Promote the session to per-item: `mk-cook-live-<scope>.items[itemKey] = {targetC, probes:[], status, devId}`. Add `state:'ok'|'fault'` to the device record. Then `scope:'live'` rules — `STALL`, `BEHIND_SERVE`, `READY_EARLY`, `DEVICE_FAULT` — emit `offer` findings whose options are Phase-3a `orchestrate()` moves, and `applyMove` re-runs `planSchedule`/`schedulePlacements`. `DEVICE_FAULT`'s options come from `cookerCandidates(kind)` minus the failed device, already filtered by `eqmDeviceMeetsRow` — their backup ladder, but capability-aware. The `READY_EARLY` option is the cooler transfer, which requires making the cooler a real device with a hold profile so it can free rack area in `schedulePlacements` and be selected by Phase-3a's `hold` rung under its existing 60°C floor / 240-min danger-zone / `holdCapMin` gates.

**Two invariants to write down and test, both derived from this comparison:**
1. *No rule may rewrite a temperature, a duration, or a safety value.* Enforced by `safetyDiff` on every rule application, not just by review. This is exactly what their rules 4 and 7 violate.
2. *Every finding is a code with primitive params; prose exists only in `renderFindings`.* Enforced by a build check that no `RULES` entry contains a string literal outside `id`/`code`/`cite`.

**Rules-coverage report** as a build artifact: every rule id needs ≥1 test asserting it fires and ≥1 asserting it does not (DoD-6's negative case, mechanised), and every `code` needs a translation in every active language (Guard A gives this free once codes live in one `L()` table).
openQuestions: Should `methodRules` itself become rows in `RULES`, or stay a per-cut-class descriptor that rules read from? I lean toward keeping it as the descriptor (it is data about the cut, not a decision) and having rules consume it — but that means two layers and the boundary needs a ruling.

`equip.alt` is authored per recipe and unread, while `cookerCandidates` hardcodes the same substitution in code. Which becomes authoritative? If the data wins, `cookerCandidates` must read it and every path/ownership verdict changes — that is a behaviour change needing full-suite proof, not a wave-0 item.

Does the outcome vector in `pathOutcome` need citations of its own? A tenderness/bark/chew score derived from cited fields is a derived opinion, not a cited fact. My position is it is safe because it never enters a plan value and only orders already-cited paths — but it is the first derived-judgement surface we would ship and the owner should rule on it explicitly.

Per-item live state changes the `mk-cook-live-<scope>` shape. Migration policy for an in-flight session at upgrade time: silently promote the single probes[] onto the first item, or drop the session? Dropping mid-cook state is user-hostile; promoting it guesses.

Should `DEVICE_FAULT` be user-declared (a 'this device is down' button) or inferred? Inference needs telemetry we do not have. User-declared is buildable now and covers the real scenario, but it is a different UX contract than the proposal assumes.

How far does the registry go before it becomes its own maintenance burden? Thirteen decision sites is too many; forty rules with a coverage report may also be too many. Worth agreeing on a stopping rule — e.g. only decisions that produce a user-visible finding become rules; pure arithmetic (eqmFitVerdict) stays a function.

The 'never render an option the engine will block' principle conflicts with our current block-at-the-gate pattern (eqmAddGate's toast). Adopting it fully would mean the catalog filters itself by kit, which is a significant UX change and possibly an owner preference call rather than an engineering one.
